To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the growth response of trees to climate change depends on the species, and the response of growth rate to warming is not only driven by the longer growing season but also by the sensitivity to extreme climatic events.

(i) the response of growth rate of beech and Norway spruce to warming depends on the sensitivity to vapor pressure deficit (VPD), which is higher for beech than for spruce; and (ii) the effect of extreme climatic events on growth rate can be accounted for by models that include VPD as a key variable.

“We demonstrated that climate warming and extreme climatic event models better explain the contrasting growth responses than models incorporating only average climatic conditions, and the contrasting responses of two dominant tree species in Switzerland to climate change are mainly due to their different sensitivities to vapor pressure deficit.”

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that climate warming can have a positive effect on the productivity of beech and Norway spruce, but that the effect is limited by the increasing frequency of extreme climatic events.
we have shown that the growth response of trees to climate change is not only dependent on the mean climate but also on the frequency of extreme climatic events.

climate warming will likely have positive effects on the growth of both species, but beech will be more sensitive to extreme climatic conditions, which will likely have negative effects on its growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the vulnerability of trees to warming and drying will depend on the species, and that the growth response of trees to warmer conditions is not linear, but rather depends on the intensity of extreme events.
the response of forest trees to climate change depends on species‐specific responses and that models using only average climatic variables will fail to predict future growth.
species‐specific responses of tree growth to climatic changes should be considered when assessing forest sustainability.
